subject: Adding data simulation to a model with custom distribution results in massive slowdowns -- advice?

messages.author: 46f76d1903dc6874
messages.subject: Adding data simulation to a model with custom distribution results in massive slowdowns -- advice?
parts:
Hi,

I'm working on a hurdle-negative binomial model. I've specified a custom distribution that combines the hurdle with the zero-truncated negative binomial so I wouldn't need to worry about control flow related to whether the data observation was a 0 or not, and to make simulation of new data easier.

The code for the distribution is appended below. I noticed that when adding data simulation to the sampler (for the purpose of posterior predictive checks) the sampler is slowed by orders of magnitude. Is there anything obvious in the code below that could be causing this slow down?

Thanks much,
Vincent


### The distribution
dhurdlenbinom <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(x = integer(),
                 p = double(),
                 size = double(),
                 hurdle_prob = double(),
                 log = logical(0, default = 0)) {
    returnType(double())
    
    ## First handle zero data
    if(x == 0) {
      if(log) {## return the log probability if log = TRUE
        return(dbinom(x, size = 1, prob = hurdle_prob, log = TRUE))
      } else { ## or the probability if log = FALSE
        return(dbinom(x, size = 1, prob = hurdle_prob, log = FALSE))
      }
    }
    
    ## If x is non-zero, use truncated nbinom
    nbinom_dens <- dnbinom(x, size = size, prob = p)
    nbinom_nonzero_prob <- 1 - dnbinom(0, size = size, prob = p)
    
    final_dens <- nbinom_dens / nbinom_nonzero_prob

    if(log) return(log(final_dens))
    return(final_dens)
  })
rhurdlenbinom <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(n = integer(),
                 p = double(),
                 size = double(),
                 hurdle_prob = double()) {
    returnType(integer())
    is_zero <- rbinom(1, size = 1, prob = hurdle_prob)

    if(is_zero) return(0)
    
    nbinom_zero_prob <- dnbinom(0, size = size, prob = p)
    
    x <- qnbinom(p = runif(1, nbinom_zero_prob, 1), size = size, prob = p)
    
    return(x)
  }
)
registerDistributions(list(
  dhurdlenbinom = list(
    BUGSdist = "dhurdlenbinom(p, size, hurdle_prob)",
    discrete = TRUE,
    range = c(0, Inf),
    types = c('value = integer()',
              'p = double()',
              'size = double()', 
              'hurdle_prob = double()')
    )))

### The model code
model <- nimbleCode({
  # Likelihood
  for (i in 1:N) {
    # negative binomial mean
    mu[i] <-  (exp(X[i, 1:n_beta] %*% beta[1:n_beta]))[1, 1] # [1, 1] is hack to
                                                             # coerce to scalar
    
    # Moment matching to negative binomial
    p[i] <- r / (r + mu[i]) 
    
    # Hurdle probability
    hurdle_prob[i] <- (ilogit(X_hurdle[i, 1:n_beta_hurdle] %*%
                              beta_hurdle[1:n_beta_hurdle]))[1, 1]
    
    # Use a custom distribution so that control flow works depending on the
    # value of y
    y[i] ~ dhurdlenbinom(p = p[i], size = r, hurdle_prob = hurdle_prob[i])

    ## Simulate new data
    y_new[i] ~ dhurdlenbinom(p = p[i], size = r, hurdle_prob = hurdle_prob[i])

  }
  
  ## Priors
  beta_hurdle[1:n_beta_hurdle] ~ dmnorm(beta_hurdle_mu[1:n_beta_hurdle],
                                        cov = beta_hurdle_cov[1:n_beta_hurdle,
                                                              1:n_beta_hurdle])
  beta[1:n_beta] ~ dmnorm(beta_mu[1:n_beta],
                          cov = beta_cov[1:n_beta, 1:n_beta])
  
  r ~ dgamma(0.0001, 0.0001)
  
  ## Posterior predictive checks
  ynew_mean <- mean(y_new[1:N])
  p_mean <- step(ynew_mean - y_mean) # pp check for mean
  
  ynew_var <- var(y_new[1:N])
  p_var <- step(ynew_var - y_var) # pp check for variances
  
  
})

messages.subject: Re: Adding data simulation to a model with custom distribution results in massive slowdowns -- advice?
parts:
Hi Vincent,

Thanks for the question and glad you worked it out satisfactorily on your own.

In many cases a good option for posterior predictive simulations is to do them after the MCMC has run.  You can do so with a nimbleFunction that iterates over the sample, uses copy() and/or values()<- to put values in the model, simulates from the model as needed, and extracts the simulated values.  An exception is if the posterior predictive values of interest depend on parameters or latent states that are not being monitored for the MCMC output.

-Perry

})

On Thursday, May 28, 2020 at 2:18:08 PM UTC-6, pdevalpine wrote:

Hi Vincent,

Thanks for the question and glad you worked it out satisfactorily on your own.

In many cases a good option for posterior predictive simulations is to do them after the MCMC has run.  You can do so with a nimbleFunction that iterates over the sample, uses copy() and/or values()<- to put values in the model, simulates from the model as needed, and extracts the simulated values.  An exception is if the posterior predictive values of interest depend on parameters or latent states that are not being monitored for the MCMC output.

-Perry
